parts:
I think what Josh means is that ltm isn't all that effective in
estimation, especially with larger numbers of items/subjects since it
doesn't seem to keep numerical accuracy well. In smaller models you
don't notice this (like the LSAT7 dataset) but larger models you
certainly will.

Also, the large discrepancy in LL values is partially due to mirt
adding in the constant term from the multinomial likelihood equation
following estimation. The likelihood that is printed to the console
when verbose = TRUE in mirt() should correspond to ltm's likelihood
(provided that it's numerically accurate....). Cheers.

Phil

On Wed, Jul 17, 2013 at 09:03:43PM -0700, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> Thanks Josh. In what way is ltm so bad (haven't really looked at the code
> closely at any point)? I know numerically it's pretty unstable, but several
> people have reported it that it matched up often with Mplus and other IRT
> software. Could you elaborate on what you've seen? Cheers.

It looks like the engine is contained in EM.R:

EM <-
function (betas, constraint, iter, verbose = FALSE) {
for (it in 1:iter) {
pr <- probs(Z %*% t(betas))
qr <- 1 - pr
dvar <- pr * qr
p.xz <- exp(X %*% t(log(pr)) + mX %*% t(log(qr)))
p.x <- c(p.xz %*% GHw)
lgLik <- sum(log(rep(p.x, obs)))
if (verbose)
cat("EM iteration:", it, " -logLik:", -lgLik, "\n")
p.zx <- (p.xz / p.x) * obs
Nt <- GHw * colSums(p.zx)
nb <- matrix(0, p, q.)
for (i in 1:p) {
ind <- na.ind[, i]
Y <- outer(X[, i], pr[, i], "-")
Y[ind, ] <- 0
sc <- colSums((p.zx * Y) %*% (Z * GHw))
hes <- crossprod(Z, (dvar[, i] * Nt) * Z)
nb[i, ] <- betas[i, ] + solve(hes, sc)
}
betas <- nb
if (!is.null(constraint))
betas[constraint[, 1:2]] <- constraint[, 3]
}
betas
}

I can't really follow what is going on here, but I don't see optim or a
bespoke Newton-Raphson so I'm not sure how parameters are updated.
Furthermore, I don't see any attention given to multiple groups.

ltm under-performed some of my early code adapted from Baker & Kim
(2004). My code didn't have convergence criteria or multigroup awareness
and it did much better than ltm on a simple simulation study:

See slide 29 of http://people.virginia.edu/~jnp3bc/dada-20121101.pdf

This code looks fine to me, the Mstep isn't done with optim it's just
a regression from the complete data table (the for(i in 1:p){} code
chunk shows a clear Newton-Raphson like update in the last line).
Looking down the function calls it looks like ltm also applies the
Bock and Lieberman method for ML estimates and is how it gets it's
standard errors, so maybe that's what it throwing things off as the
number of subjects and items grow.

messages.subject: Re: LogLik
parts:
No, they aren't necessarily due to sample size; that's the issue here.
Occasionally ltm seems to return values that are extreme when it
really shouldn't be (like discrimination parameters > 15) while other
software do not on the same datasets. Josh is correct that there is
something wrong with the implementation, and collectively we're not
exactly sure what it is.

Your question about appropriate sample size, like all statistical
questions on this kind of topic, is that it depends on a number of
variables. In statistics the general rule is usually around 5 subjects
per parameter estimated, but in IRT that's not usually the case and
often requires a lot more. Rasch models tend to require less since
they really only estimate intercept parameters which are generally
easy to obtain anyway, while the 4PL model would require sample sizes
in the thousands along with prior parameter distributions just to get
something stable and meaningful. The number of response categories in
polytomous models also plays a part, as well as the frequencies within
each category (sparse categories give little information about item
thresholds). There are several other variables that influence
parameter recovery, so much like SEM it's a complicated question that
often requires simulation studies to determine just how well IRT work
under various conditions.

Em quarta-feira, 24 de julho de 2013 03h14min10s UTC-3, Phil Chalmers escreveu:
No, they aren't necessarily due to sample size; that's the issue here.
Occasionally ltm seems to return values that are extreme when it
really shouldn't be (like discrimination parameters > 15) while other
software do not on the same datasets. Josh is correct that there is
something wrong with the implementation, and collectively we're not
exactly sure what it is.

Your question about appropriate sample size, like all statistical
questions on this kind of topic, is that it depends on a number of
variables. In statistics the general rule is usually around 5 subjects
per parameter estimated, but in IRT that's not usually the case and
often requires a lot more. Rasch models tend to require less since
they really only estimate intercept parameters which are generally
easy to obtain anyway, while the 4PL model would require sample sizes
in the thousands along with prior parameter distributions just to get
something stable and meaningful. The number of response categories in
polytomous models also plays a part, as well as the frequencies within
each category (sparse categories give little information about item
thresholds). There are several other variables that influence
parameter recovery, so much like SEM it's a complicated question that
often requires simulation studies to determine just how well IRT work
under various conditions.

>
> (mod2<-mirt(dados,2))
> Erro em ESTIMATION(data = data, model = model, group = rep("all",
> nrow(data)), :
> Too few degrees of freedom to estimate the model.
>
> I verified that there is a restriction in the model (df <- df - nestpars +
> nconstr). Why?

The reason is to avoid negative total degrees of freedom for models,
likely from estimating too many parameters in small datasets or
datasets that don't vary much between response patterns (like Guttman
scales).

> What changes for the MIRT with this changing? I would like to know it and to
> understand it a bit better.
> Before the new version I obtained these results, but now, mod2 isn´t
> calculating anymore. How should I do it?

Take a look at mod2 here, it has a total of negative 14 degrees of
freedom, which is nonsensical and provides a df difference of 29. In
previous versions I allowed this without thinking, but in recent ones
I don't. Also, it looks like your dataset shouldn't support
exploratory estimation anyway since the size is so small (90
individuals, with repeated response vectors effectively decreasing the
total df, and estimating nearly 60 slopes and 30 intercepts means that
there are more parameters to estimate than total df).
